extracted.intended_audience: improv students, workshop leaders, and performers interested in Keith Johnstone-style improvisation
extracted.subtask_description: Notes and practical exercises drawn from the first section of Keith Johnstone's Impro, focused on cultivating spontaneity, play, and removing fear in improv workshops and performance. Includes concrete exercises and pedagogical guidance for running sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage spontaneity, play and abandoning fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The first levels of training should be all about encouraging spontaneity, play and abandoning fear on stage as you explore how to improvise in its purest form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure early courses around exercises that force quick responses and physical play; emphasise play over correctness and normal performance standards. The aim is to remove the fear that prevents people attempting things in the first place ("fuck the fear").

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead by the students (avoid strict syllabus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keith dislikes formal education and strict syllabuses; teachers should be led by the students—to connect to who they are, what they want, and what is happening in the present moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce activities in response to the group's needs and interests rather than sticking rigidly to a plan. Let learning emerge so students 'don't realise they are learning until they get to the end and then they just "know".'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow what's fun in the moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Above everything else, teachers should follow what’s fun right there and then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise engagement and curiosity; if something in the room is fun or interesting, pursue it even if it wasn't planned. This keeps sessions alive and student-led.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove fear by playing lower status / de-authoring the teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing lower status (e.g., the teacher acting awkward/goofy) can remove students' fear and the intimidating 'guru' status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers can deliberately act less authoritative early on to create safety and reduce performance anxiety. Use status-play as a tool to ease participants into experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leap before you look
rubrics_metrics.description: Act before overthinking: be not careful or intellectual—'we jump and find out why on the way down.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercises where participants must start a scene immediately on impulse (see 'leap before you look' exercise). Train people to make a move rather than debate the right choice; reward emotional engagement and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less discussion, more doing
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage less talking about ideas and more getting things up on their feet and trying them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, put an exercise, scene, or game in front of the group rather than lengthily analysing. Learning through practice is emphasised over deconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to be imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't have to be perfect; fear of failure prevents attempts. Johnstone gives permission to break rules and let thoughts come without judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and encourage mistakes, unpredictability, and 'wrong' answers as creative fuel. Reassure participants that imperfect material leads to discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful rule-breaking (do the opposite of school rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnstone wrote down everything his teachers told him not to do and then did the opposite—pull faces, play with insults, crawl around like an animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercises that invert social norms to free blocked behaviour. Emphasise safety and consent, but intentionally break benign social rules to liberate play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace the subconscious and stream-of-conscious responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Value subconscious ideas as nourishing sources of creativity; let thoughts come without judgement and allow 'things we can't say in real life' to surface in controlled exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that solicit raw, uncensored material (naming, free association) and explicitly suspend judgement for those moments. Normalize unusual or taboo words as words, not moral acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming things/not-naming things exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise: run around pointing to everything and saying what it is, then run around and say what things aren't—don't question what comes, just let it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a warm-up to liberate forbidden or silly words; treat any wrong or rude utterance without judgement. The goal is to break attachment to 'use the right word for the right thing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Making faces to overcome self-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapidly make lots of different faces, then use those faces to inspire scenes—this breaks concern about appearance and frees performers to play physically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quick facial-change drills and follow-up pairing exercises (two people using their current faces to start a scene). Emphasise that letting go of how you look increases playful availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nincompoop / playful insults exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors play a scene where each line contains a playful insult and the players also react to the insult they were given. Insults are invented, mild (e.g., 'nincompoop', 'goblin's armpit'), and not personally vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep insults at a fantasy/mild-comic level and focus on the reaction—it's the reaction that sells the exercise. This frees people from fear of offending because the mode is explicitly playful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step on stage to build a relationship (focusable task)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of 'doing a scene'—which is impossible to control—ask improvisers to 'step on stage to build a relationship'; the scene becomes a by-product of that relationship work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give prompts that do not specify relationship so improvisers create relationships spontaneously (love, hate, family, etc.). This gives performers an actionable, lower-pressure objective and reliably generates scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use whole-body physicality to inspire impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors move around at random with whole-body actions; body positions can inspire lines and scenes even if they don't have to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In warm-ups and starters, prioritise movement (not just dialogue). Physical choices can create openings and emotional truth that dialogue alone may not generate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat exercises as playful experiments and adapt per group
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops are playful ongoing experiments—what works for one group might not work for another; the pursuit of play unites the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible: observe group responses and iterate on exercises. Keep the tone exploratory rather than prescriptive; modify difficulty, content, and constraints to suit the group's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'how' vs 'what' in improv pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnstone's Impro focuses on 'how' to improvise (spontaneity and play); other books (Truth in Comedy, UCB manual) focus more on the 'what'—scene and show structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Johnstone-style exercises early to develop spontaneity, then later introduce structural formats for 'what' to improvise. Combine methods as complementary rather than conflicting.
